subtopic: INDUSTRY
INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: PETROCHEMICAL INDUSTRY-EFFECT OF TAXATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and of the Minister of State for Economic Development, I wonder if I might direct this question to the Prime Minister. As we witness the tragedy of 1.5 million Canadians unemployed, the Government is floundering around looking for make-work projects. At the same time, industries such as the petrochemical sector, which could provide some 50,000 jobs for Canadians, are virtually on the brink of collapse as a result of the Government's ill-conceived and misguided energy tax policy. The problem is that it puts the Canadian petrochemical plants at a very serious competitive disadvantage. May I ask the Prime Minister when his Government and Cabinet will act to redress this very serious situation which has already cost some 8,000

December 20, 1982
Ora! Questions
jobs and has forced the Canadian petrochemical industry to operate at 50 per cent capacity?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: PETROCHEMICAL INDUSTRY-EFFECT OF TAXATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is seriously misinformed. If he looks around in the other countries he would see that the petrochemical industry in most countries, particularly in that of our neighbour, is in as bad or worse trouble than it is in Canada, and that is due to world demand, not to any tax policy in Canada. If the Hon. Member were a little more open-minded he would look at the whole industry, and not just focus on the effects of the Government of Canada's actions.

subtopic: PROPOSED LOCATION OF PLANTS OVERSEAS
PROPOSED LOCATION OF PLANTS OVERSEAS
speechtext:
The Right Hon. Prime Minister is obviously not being kept informed of what industry officials are saying. As a matter of fact they will point out that the main problem is Canada's lack of competitiveness as a result of the heavy up-front taxes, which are in the vicinity of 40 per cent to 50 per cent. The Vice-President of Union Carbide Canada Limited said, and I quote:
Our industry cannot withstand this level of front-end taxation because our international competitors are, by and large, being subjected to much lower front-end taxation levels.
He went on to say:
The petrochemical industry is at present in danger of being taxed out of existence-
Those are the facts. Madam Speaker. Furthermore, if the petrochemical industry were in such danger in the international marketplace, why is it that today Canadain petrochemical industries are actively seeking to establish their facilities in places where the fiscal environment is not as hostile, for example, in places like New Zealand, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia and Malaysia? Why is the Prime Minister overlooking that very important component, when Canadian companies are actively seeking to establish their facilities in other countries of the world?

subtopic: PROPOSED LOCATION OF PLANTS OVERSEAS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Government is fully aware of the difficult situation existing in the petrochemical industry at the present time.

subtopic: PROPOSED LOCATION OF PLANTS OVERSEAS
speechtext: Oh, come on!

subtopic: PROPOSED LOCATION OF PLANTS OVERSEAS
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition got up on the wrong side of the bed this morning. Did he have some more leadership problems this week-end? Perhaps we can leave him to his problems and get back to more serious matters. The petrochemical industry is a subject of considerable concern to the government. We have had substantial discussions with the industry during the last few months, and the fact is, that the industry is experiencing the same problems that are facing the petrochemical industries the world over. In Europe and Japan, the same problems arise and even the American petrochemical
industry has started to sell its products at extremely low prices. The Government is looking into these problems, and it should be understood there are no simple answers and no instant solutions. We shall be meeting again with representatives of the industry. The Government has created a task force within the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, which will be submitting recommendations very shortly.

subtopic: INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
speechtext: With all due respect, Madam Speaker, we have been receiving these kinds of answers for the last six months. Perhaps it is time to stop the debate and start acting. The fact of the matter is that the petrochemical industry has tremendous potential. It has the potential of producing a $10 billion trade balance and generation of at least 50,000 jobs by 1985, and the Minister again suggests that he has to sit around and talk it over with the industry. He still has not answered the basic question. Why is it that Canadian petrochemical companies are now actively seeking to relocate their plants in other countries of the world?

subtopic: INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would invite my hon. friend to examine this with great care.

subtopic: INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
speechtext: I will.

subtopic: INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
speechtext: I am happy he says he is going to examine it with great care, because there are not many other countries in the world where you can establish today-

subtopic: INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
speechtext: He just mentioned four of them.

subtopic: INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
speechtext: -a new petrochemical plant and really make money with it.

subtopic: INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
speechtext: He gave you four.

subtopic: INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
speechtext: Yes, but have the companies moved? Are they planning to invest? Or is it just, you know, word of mouth? Because the fact is that today there is a surplus of petrochemicals the world over. The problem is not that this country cannot produce, the problem is that there is no demand, or the demand is not high enough. If you go abroad and invest in another plant, you will not be able to sell any more because the problem is low demand and extremely low prices at the present time. So I challenge my hon. friend to go abroad and open a new petrochemical plant. I wish him good luck; he will probably be bankrupt before he leaves the country.

subtopic: INDUSTRY'S FUTURE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance is indicating that if in fact the world economy were booming and competitors were having difficulties, then Canadian policy would be just right. But those are not the circumstances which exist today.
December 20, 1982

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the former Chairman of Dow Chemical, Mr. Clifford L. Mort, in a recent speech in Toronto indicated that the National Energy Program was a disaster for oil and gas producers, but an even worse disaster for chemical producers. In partical recognition of that disaster, last spring the Minister, and particularly the Provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan made changes which have benefited oil and gas producers, but so far no changes for chemical producers. In view of the fact that thousands and thousands of jobs and hundreds of millions of dollars of export earnings are involved, why has there been such reluctance to make the necessary changes to save this very important industry?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am very interested in my hon. friend's speech. He is repeating the same speech, with no more foundation than it had before.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Too bad you did not listen to it two years ago.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: I remind my hon. friend that had his energy policy been implemented those same companies would today be operating with feedstocks at 100 per cent of international prices. That industry is operating today with feedstocks which cost around 85 per cent of international prices. It does benefit from a real advantage, thanks to the National Energy Program which my hon. friend is so quick to condemn. The industry has saved a minimum of 15 per cent on the cost of its feedstock by our program compared to his proposal at the time.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
That is a fact of life.
As far as the industry is concerned, I remind my hon. friend that other industries have similar problems of lack of demand, whether it is copper, zinc, asbestos or nickel-you name it. You can name all kinds of basic products in this world for which demand is lacking in every country. The petrochemical industry is facing the same particular problem. There is no magic solution to the problem my hon. friend has raised.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES IN NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, certainly pretending you are an ostrich and shoving your head in the sand is no solution to these problems.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERNAL STUDY OF INDUSTRY
REPORTED INTERNAL STUDY OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister indicated there was an internal study of the petrochemical industry being conducted by the government bureaucracy. In a recent book entitled "The Sorcerers Apprentices" by Peter Foster, the author indicated that the National Energy Program was catastrophic in its effect, at least in part due to dependence upon the advice of the same officials who are now preparing this report for the Minister. To prevent that kind of catastrophe from happening again, would the Minister make a commitment to this House to table that report, and
Oral Questions
refer it to the appropriate standing committee, to give an opportunity for critical examination of its premises so that we do not have another dozen projects go down the tube because of false assumptions and then have thousands and thousands of Canadians out of work, with bleak prospects, while the Minister stands and rings his hands over international circumstances?
We are talking about action here in Canada to address a Canadian problem; let us have some made-in-Canada solutions, not prayers that the rest of the world will save us.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERNAL STUDY OF INDUSTRY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my wish for the Hon. Member in 1983 is that he should improve his reading, to begin with. Secondly-

subtopic: REPORTED INTERNAL STUDY OF INDUSTRY
speechtext: You table it and I will read it.

subtopic: REPORTED INTERNAL STUDY OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Secondly, I am surprised that his big recommendation, after having made representations on behalf of the petrochemical industry, is for more study by a parliamentary committee or whatever he wants to set up. He does not want action; he just wants more talk and more study. I am sorry to have to recognize that.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister who, 1 thought, with admirable candour admitted last night on television that the current government job creation programs were not expected to make "a major dent" in the unemployment problem. We in this Party agree with that statement. We are really interested in the 1.5 million unemployed. What does the Prime Minister intend to do about it? speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subsubtopic: JOB STIMULATION PROGRAMS-GOVERNMENT PLANS

Madam Speaker, on the latter part of the question, the answer has already been given several times by the Minister of Finance and by myself. We have brought in some job stimulation programs to the tune of $2.5 billion, beginning last June and in the Minister's October statement, whereas the Hon. Member's own Leader suggested a job creation plan of some $1.8 billion. On that we are merely inviting him to catch up with us.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I would hope that the same headlines which indicated that Mr. Pitfield got an increase beyond six and five, if my statement proves to be unchallengeable, will carry now the fact that the salary increase was fractionally less than 6 per cent on July 1, 1982. That was effective July 1, 1982. The order was passed in recent weeks, but it is effective as of July 1, 1982. There was no other increase since April 1, 1981. That is relatively clear and simple.
As to the pension arrangements, they are somewhat more complicated, but I think I will be able to explain it either in my

December 20, 1982
Statements by Ministers
statement or in answering questions. I would read the following three paragraphs.
As to his pension arrangements, on June 5, 1979 the Government of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition passed an Order in Council setting the salary for pension purposes of Mr. Pitfield at the mid-point D-M 3 salary range. Under the former salary administration plan, the mid-point was the job rate. The Order in Council passed on November 5, 1982, some weeks ago, setting the salary for pension purposes only at the job rate of the D-M 3 had the net effect of simply adjusting the wording of the 1979 order to bring it into line with the current salary administration plan.
To put that in as simple words as possible in order that there be no misunderstanding, our Government is endeavouring to provide for Mr. Pitfield precisely those pension arrangements which the Government of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition provided for him in 1979. In other words, the same arrangement, beginning with the mid-point, that was provided by the Government of the Leader of the Opposition is provided by my Government, so the pension arrangements have not changed.
I sent the Leader of the Opposition a letter responding to his questions in the House on December 15. On Friday, December 17, the Leader of the Opposition raised additional questions in a letter to me. I will, if necessary, deal with it and answer the questions, but I hope that the preceding words I have spoken set the record straight.

Madam Speaker, I thank the Prime Minister for making a statement on motions. May I say in passing that I hope it becomes a practice to which the Government has recourse more often by its own choice, because it is very clearly a practice which can help the progress of this House by providing information.
Our concern has to do with the very confusion which the Prime Minister has indicated is inherent in the arrangement. He has given us today in his statement on motions two assurances. One is related to actual salary level and he has indicated there was not an increase in salary level since the increase which became effective on July 1, 1982 to Mr. Pitfield, as to other Deputy Ministers. It would be interesting for us to know whether there is any other form of remuneration available to Mr. Pitfield which is not classified strictly as salary, or indeed, available to any other D-M 3 level employees of the Government of Canada.
But 1 understand what the Prime Minister is saying, he is saying that any adjustment in the remuneration level of Mr. Pitfield was an adjustment which did not affect salary received but affected only pension received. In other words, it was an adjustment for pension purposes. Let me now come to that. The Prime Minister has talked about the job rate. The job rate, as he correctly said, was, under the previous classification, at the mid-point of what is called the decile levels of the Public Service, at about the fifth or the sixth point. It is not clear in my recollection exactly what the mid-point was as then defined in 1979. However, by a change in policy by this Government on April 1 of either 1980 or 1981-at least some several months ago-there was a change in definition of the job rate. The job rate which had previously been at the midlevel of the decile range now became the top level of the decile range. It moved from the middle to the top.
Mr. Pitfield, as we understand it, was being paid at the eighth decile level for salary and pension purposes up until the issuance of the November 5 Order in Council. After the issuance of the November 5 Order in Council, he was being paid at the top level, at what was called the "job rate". That is to say, there was an increase for pension purposes as a result of an action directly and explicitly applying to Mr. Pitfield. There was an increase in the remuneration for pension purposes from the eighth decile to the tenth decile.
It may be that no new money came to Mr. Pitfield now, but the question I want to have clarified is whether in fact there was an increase in remuneration to Mr. Pitfield from the eighth decile level at which he was being paid prior to November 5 to the tenth or top decile level at which he was being paid as a result of that Order in Council which affected him exclusively after November 5. That is the question which remains open.
While it has been drawn to light in regard to the case specifically of Mr. Pitfield, it also underlines the fundamental importance of having available here on the floor of the House of Commons a very clear understanding as to just what is being paid the senior public servants of the land, and just exactly what pension entitlement flows from the payments available to those public servants. That is a matter which should not be shrouded in secrecy in this House of Commons. That, indeed, is a matter which should be crystal clear to Hon. Members of the House of Commons.
The Prime Minister has indicated that, to his mind, it is not clear. Certainly to my mind it is not clear. The exchange of letters between us, I think, has not served particularly to clarify the matter. The Prime Minister can clarify the matter to some degree by first giving us a commitment to make much fuller and clearer information available to Parliament as to the salary level, the remuneration level, any other remuneration and the pension basis of public servants; and also he could indicate to us whether in fact the effect of the Order in Council of November 5 was to move Mr. Pitfield's remuneration level from the eighth decile for pension purposes to the tenth

decile, or in any event to some decile level higher than the eighth decile level.

Madam Speaker, today the Opposition says the matter is not very clear. It is certainly somewhat complicated because there has been a change from one system to another, and I will try to explain what that was. I must say en passant that the Leader of the Opposition is now expressing the hope there will be some further explanation. I would have hoped that he would have seen fit to seek those explanations before making the public accusations he did against a very senior and respected civil servant having left the service of the Government of Canada after more than 24 years or 25 years of service. But somewhat belatedly the Leader of the Opposition is now seeking those explanations.
I think I will attempt to explain them, Madam Speaker, in the following way. Until the administrative reform of 1981, there was a salary range which went from one to ten deciles, and that range encompassed the whole of the remuneration of a given public servant, an Order in Council appointee. If the servant was performing in a fully satisfactory way, he was at mid-range, at the fifth decile; if he were giving exceptional performance, he would be put at the seventh, eighth, or in some cases the ninth and, perhaps, even the tenth decile. But fully satisfactory was at the fifth decile, halfway through the full range.
In 1981 a reform was brought in, on the recommendation of the Business Council on Senior Appointments, chaired at that time, I believe, by the Chairman of the Toronto-Dominion Bank-

-Mr. Lambert, although there was a change. Maybe the new Chairman was appointed by then, I am not quite sure, but on the recommendation of that committee, Madam Speaker, a range was instituted which was in two parts. The scope of the range was about the same, in other words, it was from a certain minimum to a certain maximum. The total scope of the range was comparable to the system before, but the new system was brought in on a recommendation that the range be split in two, and that the deciles apply from zero to ten but up to mid-range; so that one who was performing in a fully satisfactory fashion would be at the tenth decile. But that was mid-range of the total range.
Anyone who was performing in a way which was more than fully satisfactory, exceptional or outstanding, whatever it was, was given a bonus, and this bonus covered the second half of the range. Indeed, Mr. Pitfield was scheduled at the equivalent of the former eighth decile, which in the new system meant the tenth decile, plus a bonus of three out of five, it was an exact equivalent. That is why my statement earlier, Madam Speaker, that we translated into the new system a classification which permitted us to reward people by putting them in fact eight-tenths or seven-tenths of the way up into the full range is unchallengable. But it was no longer the seventh or the eighth decile, it was the tenth decile plus a bonus of one, two, three, four or five. Mr. Pitfield in fact was classified at the equivalent

of the eighth decile under the old system, but under the new system it meant the mid-point plus a bonus of three out of five.
Now, for pension purposes, Madam Speaker, Mr. Pitfield would have been perfectly justified to say: "Well, this is where 1 am classified as I retire and 1 would like my pension to be based on that". But in order to prevent the kind of accusation which unfortunately was made against him anyhow by people who seem intent on destroying his reputation without foundation or knowledge, he voluntarily took a sacrifice and said; "Well, I do not want to be classified at mid-range plus three out of five, putting me at the equivalent of the eighth decile; for pension purposes, i want to be classified mid-range . Midrange, of course, is the tenth decile now, but had the Leader of the Opposition read my letter a little more carefully, the one where I thought I would make it simple for his understanding by talking of apples and oranges, he would have seen that the tenth decile is mid-range. It is not eight tenths of the range, it is mid-range.
So rather than blame Mr. Pitfield for having gotten somehow more than his due, though i would want to point out that his due in this case would have been no less than many other distinguished public servants leaving at that time in their career, he voluntarily took a reduction to the tenth decile, being once again, under the new system, mid-point in the range.
Now, I am sorry that the Leader of the Opposition has a research group in caucus which did not understand that, which did not ask for the explanation. 1 am sorry that the Leader of the Opposition did not himself ask for the explanation before pursuing his vengeance-1 know not why-on a distinguished civil servant precisely after he left the Civil Service. speechtext:
1.	Did Eldorado Nuclear Limited select an American Firm to assist in the liquidation of the Beaverlodge plant and, if so, for what reason when there are plenty of qualified and competent Canadian used-equipment dealers and plant liquidators?
2.	What form of bidding process was undertaken to obtain a plant liquidator firm?
3.	Were there bids and, if so, what were the results of the bids?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: LIQUIDATION OF BEAVERLODGE PLANT AND EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
Eldorado Nuclear Limited reports as follows: 1. Yes, ENL did select an American firm to assist in the liquidation of the Beaverlodge plant and equipment.
The American firm submitted a proposal which was clearly superior to other proposals received for the following reasons: (i) The firm included an "up front" advance payment; (ii) The firm accepted the cost of transporting the equipment from Uranium City to an Edmonton marshalling and display area; (iii) The firm provided a guarantee to purchase at Eldorado's option all the remaining equipment unsold at the termination

December 20, 1982
Order Paper Questions
of the agreement for 40 per cent of the established minimum price; (iv) The firm undertook at their cost to prepare equipment for resale including cleaning, painting and reconditioning as required; (v) The firm agreed to use Canadian labour throughout and to give preference to Canadian firms for any services required.
2.	In its search, Eldorado contacted several mining companies, suppliers of used equipment and consulted trade journals. Due to the extensive publicity given to the mine closing, Eldorado also received numerous calls from companies interested in disposing the equipment. From these discussions, seven companies, capable of handling a project of this size were selected for further discussion. These were invited to visit the mine site to view first hand the scope of the work required. All but two accepted and spent a couple of days at the mine.
The companies were then invited to tender their best possible proposals, covering all areas of concern. One company dropped out of the bidding due to their inability to meet the deadline. Of the remaining six bidders, four made personal presentations to Eldorado staff in Saskatoon to explain or clarify their proposals, while the other two expanded on their submissions by telephone. All bidders were asked at this stage if this was their best proposal and were given an opportunity to make final changes or improvements.
3.	Following the procedure outlined in part 2, all bids were thoroughly analysed. The best proposal was made by an American firm.
The other proposals were rejected for the following reasons: (i) One firm offered the lowest commission rate. However, the firm proposed to hold an auction at the mine site and offered no guarantees as to sales revenue. The logistical problems of holding an auction sale at the mine site and the risk of receiving low returns on expensive mining equipment led Eldorado to conclude this was not the best method of liquidation; (ii) One firm made an interesting proposition based on a combined public auction/private sale concept. The firm was not prepared to risk any of their own money in the venture and expected to rely on Eldorado's personnel to complement their lack of expertise in the mining field; (iii) One firm submitted a proposal similar to the successful bidder and had the experience and personnel to do the job. However, the firm expected a 25 per cent commission for their marketing contribution and was not prepared to take any risk; (iv) Two other firms did not have the resources and skills to do the marketing job required for the project and made no provision for warehouse and storage facilities.

speechtext:
In so far as the National Research Council is concerned the answer is as follows: A study has been undertaken on the "building use study of Roy Thomson Hall, Toronto", by The Behavioural Team of Toronto, on behalf of the National Research Council acting in co-operation with the Ontario Ministry of Citizenship and Culture. A final report is due on February 28, 1983.
(a)	The study is of interest to the National Research Council as part of its over-all program on the study of building performance under actual conditions of use, particularly of public assembly buildings.
(b)	Studies of crowd movement, egress, etc., demonstrate the interaction between people and the building and indicate any design deficiencies, unsafe conditions, etc. This information helps in the prediction of crowd movement in emergency conditions (such as fire) and provides a data base for building codes. It also assists the architectural profession in improving the design of hallways, stairways and ramps, doors, amenities, etc., to provide greater safety for building users and better access for handicapped persons.
Due to the considerable length of time in the development of the Roy Thomson Hall and the many specialists contributing to it, the building incorporates a number of features and concepts which are not traditional to other Canadian halls. It was considered appropriate to make a close examination of the performance of this building under actual use by the public in order to assist future concert hall designers and increase scientific knowledge related to building use.
(c)	Research programs employing social science principles and procedures for the use of architects and engineers is a fairly recent endeavour, and few companies or individuals have the background and experience to effectively undertake such studies. The Behavioural Team has had considerable experience in studying crowd movement and building performance generally, has been involved with the Roy Thomson Hall project since early 1978, is a local (Toronto) firm and was chosen for these reasons.
(d)	The study was preceded by a small contract for $5,000 to develop a work plan, detailed estimate of costs, etc. The main study will cost $32,000 of which $25,000 is the share of the National Research Council. It was a very labour intensive study so the major expenditure is the cost of labour (92 per cent of the total) for the senior consultant in the firm and technical assistants.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, December 17, consideration of Bill C-132, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs; and the motion of Mr. Hawkes (p. 21697).

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in rising to address Bill C-132, which is now before us, and the amendment that stands in the name of the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), I would like to refer back to a phrase-a quotation of a former member of this House, a onetime leader of my party, who said on a number of occasions: "Whenever they say," 'it's not the money, it's the principle of the thing', you can always be sure it's the money".
We have heard much talk during debate, during report stage and earlier in second reading, especially from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), with respect to the fact that she believes that the principle of universality and all of the principles involved in making payments to the mothers and families of this country should remain intact. But, all she is doing is taking money away while she disputes the fact that the money is leaving. However, when we look at the minutes, either of the debates in this House or of the committee, it becomes very clear that not only will the amount of payments to families across Canada and, indirectly, to the children of this country be reduced, but also it will be reduced and transferred in such a way that the moneys they do receive will come at a time when they do not need them. At least, they will not need them anywhere nearly as much as they do on a regular basis.
The Minister has also been engaged in considerable playing with figures and principles. While much of what she says sounds fine in so far as statistics or figures or abstract theories are concerned, when one gets right down to it she must be very confused or else she must think that the people of this country are very confused if they are to believe the kind of things that the Government has been saying. In the minutes of the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs dated December 7 of this year, the Minister went so far as to say that if as much as one dollar remained in the Family Allowance payment per year, that would still be a universal program. I do not know if that suggests that there is something more in store for other programs which the Minister claims will still be universal or whether universality will or will not continue in the old age pension and Old Age Security systems or in a number of other Government programs.
What does this spell out for the future? If one dollar in the Family Allowance scheme means that it is still a universal program, then if one dollar is left at some point in the basic old age pension system, will it still mean, in the Liberals' view, that that is a universal old age pension program? Just what do we have left? The Minister may not be the universal soldier,
Family Allowances Act, 1973
but she may well be regarded as being the universal "pass the buck" artist, if her description of universality stands, i would suggest to her that she ought to consider very closely that old phrase of Tommy Douglas; "It's not the principle of the thing, it's the money". At least, that is what is important to those hundreds of thousands of Canadian children in Canadian families who have relied upon the Family Allowance system for a certain portion of their regular income.
Unlike the Minister and, so she says, also the Hon. Member for Calgary West, I did not study the social sciences in an academic way in any academic institution. Thus, I do not suffer from the ivory tower handicap from which those who consider problems only from the top down suffer. I have, however, studied the social sciences from the ground floor, from the street level of society, and that living experience, coupled with a fair smattering of reading in the behavioural sciences, has not only allowed me to-in the Minister's own words-"recognize the importance of the psychological element in any economic objective or goal", but it has also allowed me, in other words, to see through this old style "now you see it, now you don't" shell game as being the PR con game and flim-flam that it really is. That is exactly what we are getting here. The Minister and the Government had admitted to the fact that this but a sword in their arsenal in their war on inflation, and if that is not a PR con job, if that is not a shell game, then 1 for one do not know what a shell game is.
If one looks at the impact of this measure. Bill C-132, a measure to partially deindex Family Allowances in Canada, and considers its impact through the eyes of Family Allowance recipients in these hard economic times-and the timing here is crucial-one cannot help but realize that it is not only a bad and unwise measure, but that it is also a measure which is occurring at the worst possible moment, both for those who normally receive it and for the economy of the communities in which they live, as well as for the economy of the country.
The Minister says that those who, in her own words, "really need help" and are eligible for the Child Tax Credit will receive an increased tax credit at the end of next year. She says that the amount of the credit will make up for what they will not receive every month as a result of the cuts in this Bill. However, the problem faced by the economy and many small businesses, as well as low-income families and mothers, is a lack of consumer purchasing power and a lack of cash flow now and in each and every month, and the receipt by families of a payment with their tax returns once a year in one, singleshot crack will not help. That method has failed. Only regular income coming in at the time that they must pay their bills will help them, particularly in the kinds of situations in which many Canadians find themselves, hopefully temporarily, at this time.
Family Allowance received every month can add up to quite a bundle. A family with three children receives approximately $80 a month. Family Allowance received every month is often the only regular cheque that many families receive, especially

December 20, 1982
Family Allowances Act, 1973
when breadwinners are laid off and on U1C or out of UIC. Thousands are being dumped off the UIC rolls every month or are on welfare. Worse yet, many are not even receiving welfare. As has been reported in this House, this is turning into a chronic situation in many communities. Many times the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) has pointed out that in the major community in his constituency, Kamloops, many people are having to go to food banks or soup lines because they fall in between the unemployment insurance system and social assistance programs. That is the only cheque that these families and many others get, and they count on it.
For a family who is "in need", as the Minister likes to describe it, a little lump sum once a year is of little help, and it is of no help if the breadwinner, as we hope, has his or her job back by the time, in the next year, that they would get the little extra that is going to be added on to the Child Tax Credit. Thousands of people every month are running out of unemployment insurance benefits but their house payments, their car payments, or just their regular bill payments, continue. That goes on and on.
Statistics released at the beginning of this month, Mr. Speaker, show that now more than one-third of the unemployed are heads of families. We now have a number of unemployed equal to the whole combined labour force of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Manitoba, fully one-half of the Provinces. Those figures also show that more than one-quarter million men and women have been unemployed for over a year. We have it on recent authority from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and from the musings of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on television last night that things are not likely to get much better; in fact, he has stated that things are likely to get worse. That means that more people who will not be eligible for a tax credit in the coming year are going to find themselves out of work and relying on unemployment insurance or worse. Just at the time that this plague is becoming chronic and people, who are used to decent incomes and good average incomes, will often end up with no income at all, the Government implements a measure which even in the best of times would be unjust.
One out of every 13 people in British Columbia will be dependent on welfare by the end of this winter if the current economic slump continues. Those figures are from statistics released by the Government of that Province. One of the problems has been that people have had to go on social assistance because the bureaucratic bungling of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has meant that either there is delay at the time they try to establish their unemployment insurance claim, or if they go on one of the quickly thought-up make-work projects that he has put them on, they end up by being dumped off the UIC rolls. It is at times like these that families, children and mothers across this country need all the help they can get. Why then has the Government, even if it could argue that at some perfect time
within its odd rationale of the concept of universality or fairness that it would be better to do it the way it has, why has it chosen this time to do it? Simply for some cooked up propaganda campaign to persuade people of the glories of six and five? It is a hell of a price to pay-

Another aspect that I want to touch on briefly is that this is an time when many Canadians, especially over the last 10 or 15 years, have been making noises, with a lot of justification, calling for the establishment of various and sundry financial schemes and Government programs that would allow women who are raising families, the homemakers of the country, to be able to regard some income as being theirs-whether a salary for homemakers, pensions for homemakers and/or other reallocation of income. The Government loves to set up commissions and conduct pension and income studies. We have had, it seems to some of us, dozens of them over the last few years. What is the purpose, however, of talking about new schemes if they now set

out, for just the picayune amount of money and savings involved, to dismantle the one program that does provide some basic and minimal incomes for the family.

That is the point at which I and my colleagues in the New Democratic Party and most social democrats and democratic socialists the world over disagree with the fundamental philosophy of the Liberals and Conservatives. We want a society with laws that give strength to people and their democratic organizations so that they do not have to rely on any Government or major corporation for hand-outs. Given the power and the ways to devise their own means of livelihood and their own structures in society, they can take control of their own destiny and get rid of the hand-outs for which this Government has been so famous, but which are done in such a terrible and wasteful way.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to discuss Bill C-132, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act. Recently 1 spoke on Bill C-91. I felt very strongly about that Bill. It seemed to give the Government powers which it should not have and it could have a serious effect on property owners in this country.
I feel even more concerned about the possible effects of Bill C-132. It is not to a great degree a threat to property owners in this country. Rather, it affects those people who cannot afford to buy property, people who are tenants, quaking in their boots that the next knock on their door might be the landlord waiting with an eviction notice.
It will be yet another slap in the face from the cruel hand of fate for single mothers, many of whom work at low-paying jobs and who perhaps do not know if there will be anything to eat for supper. Perhaps it will be the last straw for some unlucky woman abandoned by her husband and left with the responsibility for the care of her children. Such a Bill will do no harm to the lobster crowd. The Kraft dinner people will bear the burden of this, the latest in a shoddy series of so-called restraint measures by this Government.
It is not the children receiving video games under well-laden Christmas trees who will suffer this year. Rather, it is those mothers who cannot even afford the Christmas tree, let alone the gifts to surround it who will suffer. By effectively eliminating the increase in Family Allowance payments, our great Santa Claus from Sussex Drive is guaranteeing a colder, harsher Christmas for years to come, he can rest assured that Kraft dinner will be the item of choice for future dinners and that thousands of underprivileged children will continue to be nattily dressed in hand-me-downs. I understand that the price of such garments does not rise with the index of inflation.
In the last two weeks we have seen a colossal demonstration of insensitivity to the needs and wishes of the poor, the elderly and the members of the Public Service by the reintroduction of Bills C-131, 132 and 133. Although the Members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition have the utmost respect for the idea of restraint, we often find ourselves wondering why such measures often seem to be at the expense of the underprivileged members of our society.

This is not only largely unncessary but almost unconscionable in light of the poverty which afflicts many thousands of unseen and voiceless Canadians. Certainly if I require translation of a document, or if some other Member does, there should be facilities available; no one would argue that. However, to have every single word ever uttered translated into the other official language is absolutely absurd.
I could go on to list the examples of waste and excess in every facet of Government administration, but I would not want to keep Members here until past midnight. The examples speak for themselves and I need not pursue this fact any longer. To sum up my thoughts on the issue of priorities in spending, 1 would like to suggest that this Government follow the philosophy: "Do as I do, not do as I say". By showing a good example of fiscal responsibility, the citizens of this country will be encouraged to do so as well.
I am glad that I am presenting this speech at a time when the yuletide spirit is rampant in the streets and I can allude to Christmas symbols to illustrate my argument. One could compare Bill C-132 to a Christmas tree standing in the corner all bare and neglected, no ornaments on it, presenting a not very satisfying appearance. But add a few decorations and some tinsel, place a star on top, and you have a delightful spectacle. The star on top of the Christmas tree is the Child Tax Credit proposal for compensating those whose Family Allowance cheques leave them financially less well off than in the past.
No, the Government is not just leaving that bare tree for us to ignore. It is dressing it up so that we will buy it and love it. Fortunately, there are some insightful people around here who see the Child Tax Credit for what it is, a fraud. Let me explain why it is a fraud. In this latest thrilling little diversion offered by the entertainment committee of our Liberal counterparts to pacify the militant objectors to the Government's tinkering with mothers' allowance, a nice little $50 increase per child in the Child Tax Credit in the next two years is offered. This means that in the tax year 1982, the value of the Child Tax Credit will go from $293 to an astonishing $343 per child. Therefore, the Government reasons, the poor people who can least afford to pay their taxes will not have to pay out as much in tax.
The richer families in the higher tax brackets will benefit less than the poor from this amendment. Anyone making less than $26,000 will receive the full Child Tax Credit. However, there are two negative factors involved in this. The first one is that there will be another mountain of paperwork in deciphering the mathematical complexities of relating income to the amount of Child Tax Credit receivable. Add this puzzle to the other 295 pages of the Income Tax Act amendments and we should make work for a few thousand unemployed accountants across the country.
Second, the over-all cost of the program-in other words, the net result of enriching the Child Tax Credit and partially deindexing the mothers' allowance-is that the Government will spend $95 million more than it would have in 1983 and 1984 had it not touched the programs at all. Where will this $95 million come from? It will come from the middle-class citizen, as usual, the one who does not have the accountants and lawyers to find all the loopholes. He will pay, but he is also the one who will vote this Government out of power in the next election.
Changing a program with supposed beneficial results should not result in an added expenditure of $95 million. Why even attempt to change the program to begin with if the net result is going to be an added burden for the taxpayer? When the amendments to the Family Allowances Act were discussed about two weeks ago by one of our Liberal colleagues, he mentioned that inflationary trends in modern society are partly due to psychological factors. He added that that is why the central Government should take action to implement measures that will have a psychological impact, that much of the six and five program is in fact psychological.
My question to the Hon. Member is this: Is poverty psychological? Is hunger psychological? Does living at a standard well below the poverty level constitute a psychological phenomenon? I think not, and I think most Hon. Members in the House would agree with me. I think these very sad, and not only sad but real, problems are vividly and tragically lived out in countless households across this country. There is nothing psychological or abstract about these problems.
We need real, concrete and effective means of dealing with this poverty. Reducing Family Allowance cheques sent out to provide needy children with the necessities of life is not the way to go about it. We are talking about the future of this country. The well-being of our children, Mr. Speaker, must be our number one priority, and when you restrict increases in such assistance, you are in effect cutting allowances in real money due to the inflationary factor.
There has been much talk about stopping inflation. However, the battle against this much talked about enemy must start with those who are responsible for it. Are the mothers and children of this country responsible for inflation? Emphatically not. I think it is the high rollers in comfortable political boardrooms and people in overpaid Public Service posts who are playing monopoly with the taxpayers' money. It
December 20, 1982

is they who are indulging in fantastic expenditures which are not warranted or approved by this Parliament.
Not only that, but this Government, to an unprecedented degree, is allowing the development of parasitical Crown corporations. Hundreds of millions of dollars are involved here. Why cannot the cutbacks start in these areas? Then, and only then, will the taxpayer heed the Government's restraint preaching with an attentive ear. We must attack the inflationary beast in its vital organs, not scratch its ear with Mickey Mouse programs such as this. Let us impose strict controls on Crown corporations and their spending bazaars, and allow the flourishing of independent business with its spin-off effects of competition, low prices and employment opportunities which Canadians want. That is what we need.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to quote from the great sayings of that inimitable builder of our country, Sir John A. Macdonald. He said: "The great reason why I have always been able to beat Brown is that I have been able to look a little ahead, while he could on no occasion forgo the temptation of a temporary triumph". Bill C-132 is but a temporary triumph. I implore the Members of this House to look ahead a little and reject the policies contained in this Bill in order that we may yet win the battle against inflation somewhere down the line, but not crush the underprivileged in order to do so.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon 1 would like to go on record as saying that my Party will be supporting the amendment which is now proposed of dropping the 5 per cent limit on this Bill in 1984, but that we will not be supporting Bill C-132, which intends to put indexation of six and five on Family Allowances. We are fast approaching Christmas time, all of us here are aware of that, and it is unfortunate that during the very week of Christmas we are discussing a Bill which is going to cut back what has become, I believe, almost a sacred event of Canadian family life, the program of Family Allowances.
In the Christmas story as it was told by Dickens over 100 years ago, he outlined the problems of his age, but he did it in the course of a story about a Christmas Day in England. He was a critic of the free enterprise system of the times and he demonstrated that system through the person of Scrooge. He indicated the people who were making the money for Scrooge through the family of Cratchitt; and the little crippled boy, Tim Cratchitt, who was part of the Cratchitt family, represented the poor, the weak, the outcasts of society in England at that time.
During this time the Members of the House of Commons and many people across Canada will rejoice again in the story. It is a great parable. It is done in modern literature, it is done on television, it is done as a movie, but basically it was a parable about the disparity which existed in English life 140 years or 150 years ago. In this week just prior to Christmas we are playing out in another form part of that story. We have around us the great evils of recession and unemployment which are biting into and injuring the families of so many Canadians, but here in the House of Commons we are discussing Family Allowances; one of the basic ways in which families can stay
Family Allowances Act, 1973
part and parcel of Canadian life, and this Bill is going to cut back in a regressive way the income of Canadian families.
We are discussing the children. Christmas is a children's time. These are the children who some day will sit in this House of Commons, the children who some day will take over the jobs in our country, the children who will build the economy of this land. They are the ones we are talking about today. These are the ones who will have to plan the pension plans for you and me and for a lot of other people. I have discussed pension plans with some of my nephews and nieces and they tell me they are not interested in planning pension plans for me.
At a time like this it is important that our children understand the importance of having all sectors of society well looked after, beginning with them. In the England of 150 years ago of which Dickens spoke, the beginning of the industrial revolution, there was no consideration whatsoever for the care of families built into the system. If you worked in a coal mine or factory at that time, you received a certain income. It did not matter whether you were married with ten children and supported a sick grandmother, there was just that one little salary. That free enterprise system never addressed the problem. It was only then that people in Government decided that that injustice really could not continue, that there would have to be some kind of a social system so that children, people who did not have a job, the aged and the sick would be looked after no matter what happened in the economic system. That happened because of visionaries, people who saw that the economic system could not address the problems of all people.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I happen to be in my fifties and I suspect there are a lot of other people here in their fifties. My mother never received a Family Allowance cheque for me, but I do remember when the first Family Allowance cheque came into our family. It was a very important event, and it remained so every month afterwards because, as far as I can remember, it was the only money that my mother ever received directly for all the work she ever did in our family. I always look upon my family as one of the great privileges of my life. I come from an extremely happy home, one where there was great understanding and where we shared everything. But my mother never received any money directly except for this Family Allowance cheque, which made a difference in our family. It meant that we were sure in those difficult economic times that we were going to be receiving a certain amount of money each month on a certain day.
The basis of this idea, which was introduced by the CCF around 50 years ago, was to address those problems which became more clearly identified during the 1930s, problems similar to the ones identified by Dickens in his own time. So this legislation, which was finally brought in by the Liberal Government following World War II, is good, basic legislation in the sense that it addresses the needs of children and wives and mothers who receive no other basic income.

December 20, 1982
Family Allowances Act, 1973
But today, Mr. Speaker, the kind of family life which 1 had the great privilege to grow up in is not shared by many people. I am not blaming anyone, but there has been a change in the basic moral and cultural values of our society so that today there are many families which are divided, and single parents are part and parcel of our society. I do not think there is a greater amount of happiness because of this, but it is part and parcel of our society. Because of that, the question of Family Allowances is much more important now than when there was a stable basic family unit. Today, because of so many changes in our society and in our times, it is extremely important to remember that the old family structure from which many of us come and want and hope for others is not present. That is a fact. So a change which will affect the income of single parents, mothers who are looking after one, two or three children on their own, somehow or other goes against the very basic principles that were set out by this Elouse of Commons over the years for the protection of women, children and families.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I believe that there are many people sitting on that side of the House who really do not believe that this six and five legislation being proposed should apply in the area of Family Allowances. I suspect that my colleagues over here in the Progressive Conservative benches likewise do not want to see it happen. It is eating away at the basic principle of universality, whether we like it or not. It seems to me that mobilization of six and five presumes that suddenly the world will become six and five. But it does not happen.
1 have no children of my own, Mr. Speaker, so I do not have to buy a lot of things which mothers and fathers have to buy. Therefore, I do not really know the cost of a lot of things. However, I picked up the phone and called a few places to see how six and five is affecting mothers. I called a store to see about the cost of shoes, the salesperson told me that there was a minimum 10 per cent increase on children's shoes. I phoned a grocery store to find out about milk. Two litres of 2 per cent at $1.95, up from $1.79 on November 1, or 9 per cent. That is not six and five. Now, shoes in winter, milk every day, these are necessary things but they are not six and five. But it is Christmas time and winter time, and part of that for Canadians is skating in winter time. So I phoned a sporting goods store to see what the cost of a pair of skates is. Well, the man said that skates are up about 30 per cent from last year. That is not six and five. The six and five principle being used in all these Bills is to sort of mobilize the idea that inflation will be cut back. But then to put it on the backs of mothers, the unemployed, senior citizens and retired civil servants, to say that is where the cure is, is basically wrong.
So, Mr. Speaker, the reason we are protesting against the Bill is that we feel that a section of society, the Crachitts of the world, the underprivileged, are being used as a scapegoat to bring about something which is way beyond their control.
Now, if you remember the Christmas story, Scrooge was converted. Right now, during Christmas week, we still have the hope that the Scrooges across the way might be converted
and realize that all this six and five being laid on the backs of the poor could easily be turned back. The Scrooges should listen to the ghost of election 1985.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make a few remarks on Bill C-132, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973. Of course, we all know that it is another part of the six and five restraint program announced in the June budget.
We in the House may agree that Canada today is facing some very serious economic problems. We are facing a situation where the present Government of Canada has created the present economic situation. Its vast amounts of waste and expenditures have created a massive deficit that this year alone equals the total 1974 budget of the federal Government.
There is something fundamentally wrong when Members on all sides of the House are asked to address a reduction in Family Allowances to families in need. There are poor people in the country who depend upon the Family Allowance. Mothers in the low-income group look forward to these benefits. I am referring to single mothers; treaty Indians living on reserves, some of whom are in very abject poverty; our native people, some of whom are unemployed and living in real poverty situations. But the Government, with the support of backbench Fiberal Members, introduces an attack on Family Allowances which go to these people in need. Something is wrong with the thinking of any Government which would allow this to happen.
Why did the Government not look at the Family Allowance Program and work in a system which would take these benefits away from people earning $30,000, $40,000, $50,000, $60,000 and $100,000 per year? Why in God's name would the Government not look at that situation and redirect the funds? In essence, it would save more than it will save by attacking people in need by reducing their Family Allowance benefits, reducing their expectations in terms of Family Allowance payments, or reducing the real purchasing power of those cheques by $5 and $10 per child over next year and the year after.
December 20, 1982

As Members of Parliament we represent constituents, the majority of whom are living on low incomes, yet the Government is attacking that group. It will not matter a whit that it introduces six and five on Family Allowance payments to families with incomes of $30,000 per year. It will not even be noticed by people earning $50,000, $60,000 or more per year. It will really affect families with net incomes below the poverty line. Those are the people who are being attacked.
Make no mistake about it, we will not hear a hue and cry from people in the upper, the middle-upper or middle-income levels. The hue and cry and hurt will be felt in low-income groups. I ask all Hon. Members to think about this for a minute. They should travel with me to Athabasca, Slave Lake, Paddle Prairie, East Prairie or Fort Chipewyan. In the case of Fort Chipewyan, its residents pay double the price for a quart of milk as those in the cities of Ottawa, Toronto, Edmonton or Vancouver. By introducing this six and five, the Government is taking away two or three quarts of milk per month from children of low-income families. There is something fundamentally wrong.
We must address the problems as they exist. Certainly we must restrain Government spending; I am in agreement with that. Why is the Government not looking to areas where it could actually save money without attacking people in the low-income levels? Every piece of legislation in the restraint program attacks elderly people, people on fixed incomes, people on Government pensions or senior citizens. We should be making every effort possible to ensure that they live out the remainder of their lives in comfort and without worry.
What does the Government do? It introduces legislation to cut back on the fixed incomes of some of our senior citizens, and we now see it attacking Family Allowances. I am not in agreement with the present structure of the Family Allowance. For example, 1 do not believe that my wife should be receiving a Family Allowance cheque from the federal Government when I am perfectly capable of handling the expenses in my home. Then we get into the universality of Family Allowances; yes, there is a real problem there. If we do not have a universal program, then we have somebody sitting there trying to determine whether a person is in need, is a worthy recipient, meets a means test or something like that. I do not agree with that either, but there is a middle-ground somewhere. Certainly, if we had co-operation in the House and sat down in an allParty committee, we could come up with a solution to the problem.
There is no way that someone earning $40,000 or $50,000 per year should be receiving Family Allowance, but there is a real case to be made for families living in poverty or below the poverty line and for low middle-income earners. The $25 to $30 per child means that some children will drink milk, orange juice or perhaps have some fresh fruit. The Government is attacking families who cannot afford to lose $2, $3 or $4 per month per child over the next two years.
We have heard the Government described as Scrooge. I believe that the Government has serious difficulties; I truly believe it. When I look at its deficit figures and its runaway spending, they worry me. I think we have to be responsible, but
Family Allowances Act, 1973
there are ways to reduce the deficit and bring money into the coffers of the federal Government without attacking those people for which the Family Allowance was set up to help. Why is it that every policy in the restraint program hits hardest lower-income groups? Why is it not hitting the senior civil servants and some of the high-income earners in the country? Those people are willing to share, so why not take away or reduce the Family Allowance from the upper-income earners? The Government is wrong in proceeding in this way.
We should set up a tribunal or a House of Commons committee with a view to drafting legislation for the control of Crown corporations in order to examine those 300 or 350 corporations to find out how much money they are wasting. Let us determine whether they are accomplishing what they were set up to do. We should determine how much money is being spent on Crown corporations and how much of that money is being wasted. The Auditor General has said that the ability of the Crown corporations to run holus-bolus in the country without any controls has caused a hole in the pocket of the taxpayers of Canada. Indeed, it would appear that there could be collusion between Ministers of the Crown and Crown corporations so as to allow these Crown corporations to do as they see fit to meet the aims and objectives of either a Minister of the Crown or the corporation itself.
Let us remember that it is the taxpayers, including we as Members, who are paying for the Crown corporations' existence today. These corporations employ 263,000 people across Canada. Excluding the RCMP and the Armed Forces, there are more people employed by Crown corporations than by the federal Government itself. All Hon. Members in the House of Commons who represent the constituencies of taxpayers who are footing the bill have absolutely no control over those Crown corporations in which millions and millions of dollars are involved.
Instead, the Government introduces a six and five program that attacks the mothers, and the families in the low-income group by nailing them and reducing their Family Allowance by $3 or $4 per month over the next year and the year after. Where is the priority of this Government? I am sure that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) does not agree with this. I am sure that she would not agree without strongly voicing her opinion to her Liberal caucus.
As I have indicated, I believe that a reduction of $3 or $4 in Family Allowance benefits does not concern those earning in excess of $30,000 per year, but it does concern many of my constituents who live in isolated communities. I have visited some homes in those isolated communities. Believe me, there is no turkey for Christmas and there is no meat on the table. Last summer 1 visited an elderly lady in one of those isolated communities. She is a grandmother who is supporting three grandchildren on her pension and Family Allowance. Although she was supporting three children, she could not receive social services or welfare because she received a pension. I do not exaggerate for a moment when I say that there was not even a crust of bread in that house when I visited her. All that the children were eating was relish from a gallon jar that she was

December 20, 1982
Adjournment Motion
able to pick up. She could not afford any more since it was three days until her cheques arrived.
Those are the kinds of people we are allowing this misguided Government to attack when we permit it to cut back on Family Allowances for lower-income families. 1 see some Members smiling who believe that this is simply rhetoric. It is not rhetoric. This is exactly what is happening in the country. It is wrong and all Hon. Members know that it is wrong.
There is another way to deal with the problem. A system can be devised whereby the universality of the program can be maintained with those in the upper-income bracket being taxed 100 per cent on their Family Allowances. This money can be returned to the Government. When tax returns are submitted at the end of the year, it can be determined whether the taxpayer is entitled to the Family Allowance.
Let us provide the aid where it is needed. We should determine how much money can be saved from Crown corporations. As well, we should review our own operations in the House of Commons to determine what savings can be made here. One can see the waste that occurs here every day. One only has to walk up and down the halls of the House of Commons to see the thousands of dollars which could be saved every week on the amount of printed recycled paper which flows through my office and i am sure through the offices of all Hon. Members.
When a business gets into trouble and does not have enough revenue to cover its expenditures or to pay its bills, it looks at ways to cut back in all areas. It does not simply disregard areas which may only save $20 or $30 but considers everything. A business reviews its expenditures and then curtails its expenses. That is what we should be doing, determining how we can curtail expenses in every department. We cannot curtail expenses by attacking Family Allowances, particularly for those in the lower-income levels. Those families depend on that monthly cheque.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am rather saddened to have to rise to speak to Bill C-132 and the motion which was moved by the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). This is the time of year when we look forward to joining with our friends and families. It is a time for children, a time when we reflect on the year past and what is coming up. It is not the time of year when the Government ought to be trying to jam legislation through the House to grab money out of the hands of the mothers and children of Canada. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext: The Grinch.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext:
Here is an individual who is presumably suggesting that the mothers and children of Canada are some of the critical inflation creators in this country, or that, by cutting back on the income to children, we can make significant savings for the Government of Canada.
Let us examine those two premises. First, we find that the amount of money that we are considering, in 1982 terms, amounts to $26.91 per month per child. In other words, the children of Canada receive a cheque through their mothers, on a monthly basis, up until age 18, for $26.91. The Minister of National Health and Welfare says that this must change, that we must reduce the money going to mothers and children in Canada. I would ask, why on earth would anyone put forward that proposal?
December 20, 1982

We hear from Hon. Members opposite and the Minister herself that, well, this is part of the Government machete to hack away at inflation in this country and that, in fact, by introducing the six and five program to Family Allowances in Canada, it will cause a significant dint in the rate of inflation. Does anyone really believe that the mothers in Canada, who receive $26.91 a month for each child, represent that group in society which has created and fueled this inflationary rate?
When one considers the statistics put forward by Statistics Canada, one finds that 900,000 children in this country are living below the poverty line as defined by the Government. The mothers of Canada and their 6.7 million children under the age of 18 have not created inflation in this country. If we are serious about the inflation creators, we must start considering some of the sloppy Government spending which the Auditor General brought to our attention a few days ago. We must also consider Government agencies which have now been unquestionably identified as the major creators of inflation and which have allowed increases to occur far beyond the rate of inflation, far beyond the typical wage and salary settlements of workers across this country. We must consider how the banks fell over themselves in the pell-mell rush to encourage people to spend and to borrow in the late seventies, in 1980 and in 1981 and, as a result, made massive profits, embarrassingly large profits, and then said, of course, that it was in our best interests to have interest rates of 20 per cent to 22 per cent. They said that was the best thing to happen to Canadians, that same year that the banks of Canada made such massive profits.
We must consider the corporations which borrowed beyond their means and, indeed, individual Canadians who borrowed beyond their means, jumping at a chance to expand their operations without having the necessary capital-debt ratio in hand. I suspect that many of us in the House know of individuals who ran out and borrowed beyond their means to cash in on this inflationary mad dash in an effort to make quick profits. Among these were real estate operators who were Hipping properties, daily in some cases and weekly in others. These were the individuals who fueled the rate of inflation, not the mothers and children of Canada.
For the life of me, I cannot imagine why on earth the Minister of National Health and Welfare would be fighting inflation on the backs of Canada's mothers and children. However, 1 suppose one could make the case, if one stretched logic to unimaginable limits, that, indeed, by capping the increases on Family Allowance payments and by readjusting the Child Tax Credit limit, it would save the Government of Canada money.
However, when one carefully considers the data and calculates what savings will accrue to the Government of Canada, it becomes very interesting. The reduction in Family Allowances will indeed save the Government $320 million over the next two years. However, the increase in the Child Tax Credit will cost the treasury $250 million. If one also calculates the tax loss which will result in the reduced incomes based on the Family Allowance cutbacks, one finds that, indeed, there will be a tax loss to the Government of Canada amounting to about $60 million over the two-year period. Calculated together, we
Family Allowances Act, 1973
find this six and five capping on Family Allowance will save the Government $10 million over the next two years. That is the financial saving, $10 million over the next two years! That is the price of the wings of one F-18, the value of keeping three or four Senators in place, or the cost of one of the small grants to the multinational oil companies.
One could go on and on concerning the ways and means of seeing this $10 million saving in some context. Good grief! The Government probably spends that amount in three or four weeks on advertising or propaganda, yet that is not where we are seeing the cutbacks. We are not seeing the cutbacks in areas where Government spending could be drastically reduced. Yet we are seeing the Government cutting back on the money going to Canada's mothers and children.
It becomes obvious, then, that the six and five inflation argument is invalid, that the mothers of Canada have not created inflation. If we consider the savings to Government argument, we find that that no longer is appropriate. Obviously, a $10 million savings is hardly reason to bring this kind of program into place. One must closely consider the rhetoric we have heard, particularly from Hon. Members opposite. They say: "We must all share in this six and five program together; it is something we are asking all Canadians to embrace". It is one thing to ask a person with an income of $90,000 to participate in the six and five program, but quite another to ask a single parent trying to raise two or three children and not receiving any decent maintenance payments to restrict her income as well.
The participation in the six and five program of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, herself or any other Minister, will only result in an increase of their salaries next year of $5,400. How many mothers in this country would love to have that as a total package? I think the greatest irony of all is evident when one considers one of the individuals who has been touring the country, talking up the benefits of the six and five program and the need for sharing and caring together, Mr. Ian Sinclair, the chairman of the board of Canadian Pacific Enterprises. He said: "I will volunteer as well; I am prepared to reduce my salary next year to only a 6 per cent increase". For him, of course, that will mean that he will receive an increase of $46,000 next year. But he is prepared to share.
There is no fairness in the way this program has been introduced. Certainly, one can say that as a result of this unfairness, it is the lowest blow of all. It is the lowest political blow that a Government could conflict to ask those who are powerless in terms of lobby groups and so on, those who do not have an effective voice in Parliament in many respects, the children of Canada, to bear this kind of burden.
