Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat ashamed that in 1982, in a country with the resources that we have, that I have to stand up and defend Family Allowances, the universality of Family Allowances and the whole principle that the children of Canada should take priority in this country for Government expenditures.
I would like to consider why we are in this position. The situation, I think, was signalled approximately a year ago when a parliamentary delegation went to Europe and I had the pleasure of being with that delegation to visit a number of European organizations. One of those organizations was the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. I suppose the signal was given then, and maybe I was remiss at the time in not really seeing the significance of the presentations that were given to us by people associated with the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development.
One of the things we were told at that time was that for Canadian, U.S. and West German workers in the western industrialized nations, the benefit packages were too rich. We were told we ought to consider our role with regard to world
December 20, 1982

competition and how those benefits affect the prices of commodities in world trade. Those packages which include holidays, benefits for health care and working conditions were not the cause of unemployment in the western world.
Today some nations have taken action to reduce those benefits to workers. We must consider whether those benefits such as pensions, holidays, working conditions and Family Allowances led to the decline in trade in the western world or whether there were other factors.
Who is controlling the destiny of workers in the western world, Canada in particular? Is it Government, Government policy, the financial institutions which are becoming so powerful, or the multinational corporations which have access to and expenditure of capital? Is it the Federal Reserve Bank in the United States or the Bank of Canada which has led to the situation where Members of Parliament are now in this House to debate whether the Family Allowance increases should be kept to six and five over the next two years? Is it Government policy or is the policy which led to the high unemployment in the western world a policy generated in the United States by the Federal Reserve Bank and the administration there, supported in Canada by the Conservative and Liberal Governments?
That interest rate policy has driven a great number of businesses into bankruptcy, caused massive unemployment and the loss of homes, farms and fishing vessels. That policy, which was to cool inflation by high interest rates and monetarism, has carried western nations, including Canada, to the point that we now have such difficulty that we do not know how to balance budgets and put people back to work. In fact, we are starting to attack those least responsible for inflation more than anyone else.
I have talked about the old age pensioners whose pensions will be deindexed over the next two years to six and five. As well, we are attacking the retired public servants, RCMP personnel and Armed Forces personnel who paid for their pensions and made extra contributions. The Government is attacking them because it does not know where else to go. Obviously the federal Government has no indication and cannot indicate to Canadians how long we will be faced with high inflation and high unemployment.
Bills C-131, 132 and 133 have attacked the basis of social programs in this country. They have put into question the principle of universality which this Party fought for and so adamantly supports.
Public servants were the first to feel the wrath of the federal Government under Bill C-124. Their salary increases were capped at six and five with the whole-hearted support of the Conservative Party. The atmosphere in Canada allows Governments to attack programs which in the past have been very beneficial in an electoral sense to the Liberal Party. They were brought in at the insistence of the public and in some cases at the insistence of the New Democratic Party in a minority Government situation.

I sense in my riding a certain amount of support for the six and five program. That is because people are afraid of losing their jobs. They have gained the impression that the only way out of the situation is for Canadians to sacrifice even more. It is not bad enough that we have 15 per cent unemployment in the area I represent or a national average of 12.7 per cent. What is even worse is that those who are employed are afraid of losing their jobs. They are rightfully afraid because of growing unemployment in this nation.
In my Province of British Columbia there are an estimated
100,000	people on social assistance and far more than that are unemployed. There is a growing fear in Canada, caused by high unemployment, high inflation and uncertainty, about the plans of this Government to alleviate the problem.
There is a willingness and an acceptance of the fact that by and large public servants do get too much money, that their salaries should be controlled, that senior citizens do not need total indexation any longer and that Family Allowances are no longer as important as they once were. Mothers who count on the Family Allowance cheque will have to sacrifice in this battle against inflation. We are proud that there is a willingness in our communities to create employment through makeshift and temporary programs. They are making the best of the little bit of money that goes into those communities which suffer very high unemployment.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) likes to indicate that unemployment is coming down because of the six and five program. Inflation is not coming down because of some mythical six and five program which only affects those segments of society such as public servants, Family Allowance recipients and old age pensioners. The six and five program is not working because of the Government's advertising campaign. It is working because the forest industry in British Columbia and the mining and manufacturing industries across this country are on their knees, there is massive unemployment and a massive lack of confidence in the Canadian economy. Those who are lucky enough to be working are putting their money in the bank and saving it because they are uncertain about their job security. We have a recession, if not a depression, in this country.
I am not sure whether the Government knows how to get out of it. The six and five program is simply a PR gesture to satisfy those who are unemployed. It wants them to think it is doing something. However, it is not creating employment or confidence.
The amendment to Bill C-132 before us will be supported by my Party, not because it is all that important and gives the Government one year on this program, but because it might be a slight improvement to the Bill.
This attack on universality and on Family Allowances could only come about now because Canadians are grasping at anything to improve the economy of this country and the situation in their households. It could never have been imposed by this Government unless Canadians had such fear that it would not go away. Their position, I think, was adequately indicated on Bill C-124 on Public Service wages and in their eargerness to have those capped at six and five. Therefore, I do not think they are really fooling anyone in this Party as to their real motives on these particular Bills.
The Family Allowances which goes to mothers is used by them to provide for young children, whether in the form of food or clothing, or maybe even to provide their children with some social experience they would otherwise not be able to have. I think it is important that children in our country be not only well fed, well clothed and well sheltered, but it is important for them to have some experiences, whether cultural or recreational in terms of sports or arts and crafts. Mothers should be able to have within their own income some access to money to provide an opportunity to take their children to swimming lessons, or art lessons outside of school, and to provide those kinds of experiences which children of parents with higher incomes accept as something natural in their homes. That is not always true of low-income families. It is certainly not true of single-parent families where mothers, if they are working, are normally not in highly paid occupations and have to scrape any kinds of money they can together to provide for their children. The principle of universality in Family Allowances is something that we in this House of Commons should not have to be debating. It should be sacrosanct. The mother's allowance, which is basically the only income she has in many cases, goes to the upbringing of her children.

with it or its intentions, or its eventual contribution if, indeed, accepted, but at this time the Government has an opportunity to change its mind on Bill C-132. It is not a Bill which is going to gain a great deal of revenue for the Government, but it is going to do irreparable harm to the principle of universality and it jeopardizes the whole concept of universality, not only for Family Allowances, but for pensions. And if the Government gets away with the Bill before us now, there is nothing to stop it from whittling away at other social programs and cutting back on expenditures just at a time when this society needs these programs to support families, senior citizens and all Canadians. I would implore the Government to reconsider what it is about to do under Bill C-132.

I think that the savage attacks on the indexed pension plans by open-line hosts, employers and others, are shoddy and fraudulent. I believe that full indexation is crucial because without it our incomes would fall in proportion to the inflation rate. I first learned about the word indexing from Robert Stanfield when he was the Leader of the Tory Party. He recognized, as did his Party, that unless indexation was provided each year, incomes would fall in proportion to the inflation rate, which is unfair. Simply put, without indexing, the dollar that I or my constituent received last year is really only worth 90 cents this year since the inflation rate is running at approximately 10 per cent, in five short years, with the value of a person's dollar being reduced by 10 per cent, the dollar would only be worth 65 cents. This means that the dollar is shrinking to the point where people earning the same income fail to receive the same purchasing power. Therefore, I am opposed to deindexing on a matter of principle.
Indexation is the only way one can protect oneself from the ravages of inflation. That is why I and my Party are absolutely opposed to the Government's capping proposals under Bills C-131, C-132 and C-133.
The main argument against indexed pensions seems to stem from the opinion that while Public Service pensions, whether federal, provincial or through Crown Corporations pensions, are indexed, the majority of private pension plans are not. Instead, we should be encouraging indexation in the private sector. This is where the problem presents itself. Many private pension plans exist on an actuarial assumption that if one spends his entire working life investing in the high cost dollars, due to inflation, one should happily retire and be paid back, in cheap dollars. We do not believe that that is acceptable or equitable.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to speak on the amendment to Bill C-132 which attempts to reduce the effect of the six and five program on Family Allowances. I think that most Canadians know that the Government is attempting to reduce the indexation of those programs to a level of 6 per cent in 1984, and 5 per cent in 1985. The Family Allowance program has been with us since 1944. It is a unique program because it recognizes the cost of parenting and the role society ought to play in that cost. The program was a good idea, but it has had some problems and 1 want to spend a little bit of time reviewing those problems.
There have been a number of articles in the press recently the conclusion in which has been that it costs approximately $500,000 to raise a child in today's society. That is made up of the actual out-of-pocket expenses, extra hours of unpaid labour, and it includes the income forgone by the mother when she stays home to raise the children. The recognition of that contribution, and in recognition of the great asset society has in its children, we have the Family Allowance Program. It is not a great deal of money, but it has made the point that society is taking part in the raising of children because they will be assets to the economy in the future.
From 1945 to 1973 the amount per child was approximately $7.50 per month. In 1974 it was upgraded considerably to $20 per child, while at the same time making it a taxable benefit. In addition, it was indexed so that we now have a Family Allowance in the $27 per month range, although there have been interruptions to that indexation. I believe it was 1976 that indexation was stopped as an economy measure. This time it is being stopped to fight inflation. Without these interruptions it would be almost $40 per month instead of $27, and now we have a proposal to reduce the indexation to near six and five for the next couple of years.
I am not convinced, Mr. Speaker, that doing this will do anything to fight the inflationary psychology, which is the government's argument. 1 will just quote briefly the Minister of National Health and Welfare's (Miss Begin) explanation of the Government's argument. In a committee hearing she said the idea was to mobilize all Canadians in fighting this battle against inflation. So apparently we are in a war on inflation. A few years ago we were simply wrestling with it, but now we are mobilizing all Canadians, right down to the new-born babies. Everyone is in the act. The Minister said this:
The government's philosophy in the Cabinet discussion, which is what you want to understand, was made like this: In the June budget, we decided we had reached the time where the phychological dimensions of the too-high inflation we were witnessing in Canada had to be recognized and dealt with by another psychological weapon, which was a sword-
I never studied psychology very extensively, Mr. Speaker, but I do not recall the sword being a great weapon in the understanding of psychology. Apparently it is now with the six and five program. She goes on:
-and I know the words might make you smile-a sword of a national campaign of solidarity of all Canadians, mobilizing all Canadians toward cutting in half the forecasted rates of inflation of 12 and 10 to 6 and 5. It was an arbitrary-to my knowledge-choice of common purposes for Canadians to try to embark all partners into, as I said-
Well, anyway, the mobilization has gone on and I am not sure just what it is doing. It seems to me that it is having a very real effect on the incomes of the very low income people. We are told later on, in a testimony she gave, that there are about 900,000 children who are living in poverty, whose mothers need every cent of the child allowance to give them food-not just clothing or education or trips to the movies, but food. These are the people we are mobilizing to fight inflation.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, to be a phony war. We are fighting inflation at the same time that we are increasing unemployment. It is very likely that a great many of those
900,000	children are being raised by single parents, usually the mothers, who are on welfare. A reduction affects such people in a very real way. Along with its fight against inflation, the Government has been reducing expenditures on items which create jobs. Some people who have fathers in their families are finding that their fathers are unemployed as well. The Government is busy fighting inflation, but at the same time it is creating a situation where the demand of 20 per cent to 25 per cent of the population is being cut to the point where adequate nutrition is difficult to obtain. Also this group is faced with reducing some of its other wants and is having problems finding enough jobs.
Many witnesses appeared before the hearings of other committees. They told us that what was wrong with the country was the lack of demand, yet the Government reduces the incomes of people who will create some of the demand. It is a very backward way of going about it from an economic point of view. From a social point of view, it is abhorrent to reduce incomes, no matter how slightly, for people attempting to live on these kinds of income.
I see no justice in it. I see no way that it can be justified in terms of philosophy or rational thought. It makes no sense from an economic or social point of view. It is a reversal of a longstanding policy which has attempted to assist and recognize the role women play in raising children.
I should like to refer to some of the testimony by the Ottawa-Carleton Low Income Support Service group when it appeared before committee to reinforce the effect this reduction will have upon low-income people. It pointed out that monthly Family Allowance cheques are extremely important

to the people it represents and that any reduction, even SI per month, would be keenly felt. For those who need these monthly payments just to get by, the increase in the Child Tax Credit, while welcome, will be received in a lump sum at the end of the year and will not help them to meet their monthly expenses. The reduction in the Family Allowance benefit will hurt these people very much. The following testimony appeared:
We also need to keep in mind the number of families who are separated, not officially on paper, so again for those mothers who are living on their own with their children, may have no maintenance payments and any money they get may be very sporadic, and they are in great difficulty because they do not classify for any other social benefits because on paper they are married and thereby should be receiving part of the father's income and, indeed, may not be.

I guess what I could basically talk about is a case example based on a single female self-support parent with two children under the ages of ten who lives basically on $7,000 a year through the provincial federally-sponsored social assistance system which is called family benefits allowance. Under that system, the woman receives a cheque once a month. Now that cheque once a month, I mean basically trying to exist on $7,000 within the Ottawa-Carleton area with the current housing shortage, etc., and the price of food, is impossible at best. That family allowance cheque is not a frill. It is something that puts food on the table and also that family allowance cheque is not something that pays for Christmas presents or for extras. It is absolutely for food.
I think we have made the point that the allowance is absolutely necessary for a large chunk of the Canadian population. The allowance has been attacked a number of times for a number of varying reasons. When it comes right down to it, the main reason for it was to attempt to save money.
During second reading debate we heard the Minister contend in the House that the Government would be saving $320 million over the two-year period for which Bill C-132 would exist. However, deducted from that amount was $250 million, the two-year expenditure on the Child Tax Credit. Thus the real saving is only $70 million. The Government should take note of the fact that forgone revenue, such as the gross payment on Family Allowances, was not included. The federal Government should also take into account that it will be losing those tax revenues. As a rule of thumb, the Department of Finance uses an average marginal rate of between 18 per cent and 20 per cent. If we multiply the $320 million, which the Minister said the Government will be saving, by 18 per cent to 20 per cent, we will find that the federal Government is only losing about $60 million over that two-year period. In reality, the savings from this program will be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $10 million. It is hardly worth the disruption caused, the avoidance of the recognition of the part women play in raising families, or the extra stress which very low income families will be placed under by living in an inflationary world and having their Family Allowance benefits reduced.
For those reasons we will be voting against this Bill. We will support the amendment before us at the moment to set it back, inadequate though it may be since it assumes that the Bill will pass. It simply reduces some of the effects of the Bill. We will support the amendment as a stop-gap measure, but we will oppose the Bill in any way we can.

The main reason for this legislation is the level of inflation and the consumer price index. Measures such as this would not be necessary if inflation were at 6 per cent or 5 per cent, as it is and has been in other countries.

Members to understand is that we are faced with this situation today because the Liberal Governments have led us to this point as a result of their many and various programs which they have introduced since the late 1960s. Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a couple of points relating to a question I asked in the House. I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) how he could justify a price increase in milk, which resulted in a 40-cents per package increase, at a time when families were having a difficult time putting enough food and milk on the table to feed themselves.
The businesses that packaged the milk were also experiencing some financial difficulty. They expressed some concern about this added cost due to the fact that this Government is forcing metric by Order in Council on not only the three sectors, but on the milk producers as well. The Minister's answer was nothing; he did not even discuss milk he discussed

December 20, 1982

a petition which had been presented in the House of Commons and I will deal with that at a later date.
What I would like to deal with now are some of the facts which would substantiate a concern on the part of the people of Canada over the likelihood of an increase in the price of milk because of our change from quarts to litres. I would first like to refer to an article from the Toronto Star under the headline "Metric Conversion May Boost Milk Price". Dean Archer, a chairman of the Ontario Dairy Council, is quoted in this article. He said:
It is going to cost us a lot of money to make the change-
Those expenses are going to have to be either swallowed or passed on to the consumer. And it's been my experience that if they're swallowed today, they'll just be passed on at a later date.
He also said "We really don't know whether we'll succeed," in the fight against the ... legislated change to metric.
He said the new milk packages will probably cost about 40 cents more-
Even if the increase is not passed on at this point in time it will mean a price increase at a later date. Then his last remark here:
Shoppers sure aren't going to like that-
That was the chairman of the Ontario Dairy Council.
Let us take a look at the industry. I have here an inter-office memo signed by one of the commissioners of the Metric Commission, a Mr. S. Volk, sent to Mr. Boire, who was Executive Director of the Metric Commission. The document states:
1 called Mr. Lowe, President of Beckers Dairies to review information contained in the above newspaper article.
Mr. Lowe stated he had never seen or heard of the article. He was extremely upset that metric conversion was being forced on his industry by federal bureaucrats, including MCC and Agriculture Canada. He contended there were no benefits for the consumer resulting from the conversion of milk. It was his belief they were being "cheated and ripped off' with the conversion of milk and food products.
He tried to explain that it was a voluntary process and he used as an example the Ontario Dairy Council. Well, there is nothing voluntary about it, Mr. Speaker, because the Ontario Dairy Council is the group I just quoted which is complaining about being forced to go into metric packaging.
He goes on to say that he has since resigned, and due to pressures from the Metric Commission he is resigned to the inevitability of metric bag milk. The president then went on to say:
Yes, and it's all because of metric conversion.
It continues:
Judging from the extremely hostile reaction my call solicited from Mr. Lowe, he is not a strong advocate of metric conversion.
He concluded his remarks stating he could supply the names of all the company presidents who are against conversion-with whom he dialogues daily-and maybe he should be "hollering from the rooftops more often".
It is grossly unfair of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to call a press conference and say that the move to metric is voluntary except in three sectors, that of gasoline, home furnishings and measured, weighed-out grocery produce because it is obviously mandatory in the milk packaging industry as well.
It should also be noted how grossly unfair it is for the present Government to indiscriminately allow people to use imperial measurement in some parts of the country and at the same time to harass and threaten the same type of retail outlet in another part of the country. It should be noted that in Eckville, Alberta, it is okay to sell in gallons, which they do. Consumer and Corporate Affairs banded the weigh scales and then removed the bands after a period of time and allowed the retailer in Eckville, Alberta, to go ahead and sell in gallons. He is still selling in gallons today, two and a half years after he started to do so.
It is unfair that they threaten prosecutions in Toronto, Etobicoke and Mississauga for selling in gallons, while allowing it to occur in the Province of Alberta. I suggest that that is probably because the Premier of Alberta has asked his Attorney General to defend anyone who is prosecuted for using imperial measurements.
It is grossly unfair of the Government to threaten to prosecute in the Province of Alberta against a retail carpet dealer who has the nerve to sell her carpet in both metric and imperial measurements, while at the same time to ignore dozens of retail outlets in the City of Toronto which advertise daily in the Toronto papers with floor coverings in 12 foot widths and prices per square yard. Sears Limited of Canada has advised the Metric Commission in writing that there are the dealers in Richmond and in Vancouver that have been selling and are continuing to sell in yards, while at the same time the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said he would proceed to prosecute maybe a dozen, maybe only ten, who are violating the Order in Council.
Not only has Parliament been misled, but the people of Canada have been misled by a Minister who refuses to acknowledge that the process of moving to metric in Canada is difficult at a time when the United States is moving back to imperial. They just converted 19,000 Shell service stations in the United States back to gallons; they just completed it this week. Chevron and Amoco are following suit. Why do we not get the true story out to the people, that an irresponsible Minister refuses to admit the inevitable, that it is too difficult for Canada to be forced into metric at the consumer level at a time when the United States is going back to imperial?

The industry committee which planned the conversion agreed that the single-quart container would be replaced by one litre, the two-quart container by two litres and the three quart container by four litres.
The key to the planning process for metric conversion in every sector of the economy has been for the industry to ensure a cost efficient and economic conversion. In the case of the dairy industry, because the majority of three-quart sales were at the time in the form of returnable plastic jugs, the industry wanted to be able to use up its stock of three-quart jugs before switching to the four-litre size. Therefore, the conversion to the four-litre size was delayed.
It is not as if we are imposing a draconian change or rule or sudden cost upon the industry. This is something which goes back probably eight or nine years. The conversion, furthermore, of all other container size of fluid milk in Ontario was finished by 1979. That is, the one-litre and two-litre containers have been in use for three years. It is now only four years later that the conversion to four-litre containers is being completed. The date for the conversion, or deadline, is April 1, 1983, again allowing milk processors and dealers sufficient official notice of this long awaited change.
If you understand the simple economics of increasing the volume of the container size, you will realize that if four litres is 17 per cent larger than three quarts, there must be a corresponding increase in the cost to the consumer. I thank you for the opportunity to set the record straight.

subtopic: FINANCE-ENERGY TAXES PAID BY FARMERS. (B) APPLICATION OF FARM EQUIPMENT PURCHASE TAX CREDIT
FINANCE-ENERGY TAXES PAID BY FARMERS. (B) APPLICATION OF FARM EQUIPMENT PURCHASE TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to get further elaboration on a question which I posed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on December 7. The basic issue I raised in the question concerned the amount of money that was coming from the agricultural sector, that is the farmers across Canada, into the pockets of the federal Government as a result of the increases in energy prices which had taken place since the February, 1980 election.
Just for farm fuels alone, gasoline and diesel fuel, at least an additional $300 million has come out of the pockets of Canadian agricultural producers and into the federal treasury. The Government has argued that this is not taxation but another form of revenue. However, that was not the point of my question. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has given that answer.
The essential point is that this money is being taken at a time when the agricultural sector is facing a great amount of
Adjournment Debate
pressure. It is possible that the net farm income will go down as much as 30 per cent in some sectors and decrease by 15 per cent over all. Bankruptcies will probably reach 400 this year which is a level that has never been approached before.
Despite all these occurrences, the Minister of Finance responded by talking about the prices that the Conservative Government of 1979 was considering. He also went on to deal with other matters. These did not concern the point of my question. Matters concerning the Conservative Government of 1979 are irrelevant at this time. Certainly, we did not have a signed energy agreement, which the government has pointed out.
What is important is that the Minister of Agriculture has promised energy rebates. Our agricultural sector is presently paying approximately 40 per cent of its energy costs to the federal treasury. That sector is in difficulty and needs to be considered as a primary producer similar to the petrochemical industry. There were questions asked today concerning that industry which is currently not building plants or creating jobs for Canadians because the up-front taxation that the federal Government is taking from the feedstock prevents that industry from being competitive in Canada. That industry is looking elsewhere. Because of the world recession and over all problems in the petrochemical industry, it will not be expanding in the near future.
The manner in which the Government establishes prices at this time for the agricultural sector and petrochemical industry, which produces fertilizer for agriculture, can have an influence on the regeneration of our economy. If we cut them off, if we make it impossible for them to be competitive or put additional pressures on them so that they fail, we will not have that recovery in the economy. We will continually depress our economy with resulting loss of jobs, loss of the productive ability we should have in Canada, and we will never get anywhere. We are, therefore asking the Minister of Finance to consider the energy tax rebate for agriculture which the Minister of Agriculture repeatedly promised, particularly during election time.
I was asking the Minister of Finance whether or not he would respect the promise of cheap gas and oil which he made to all Canadian consumers. His response was that he knew it was hurting, but he would not do anything about it. He went then into a long diatribe about what might have been otherwise, but that is really not the point. I would like to hear what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher) has to say.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-ENERGY TAXES PAID BY FARMERS. (B) APPLICATION OF FARM EQUIPMENT PURCHASE TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the reminder from the Hon. Member that no one likes taxes, and I agree with him. No one does like taxes. However, I would hope that someone in the House would apply somewhat better logic, and would to distinguish between tax forgiveness on the one hand and

December 20, 1982
Adjournment Debate
genuine economic activity on the other. We will not automatically create a regeneration of economic activity by forgiving taxes. The Hon. Member has used that argument but 1 must differ with him on that point.
The role of farmers, across Canada, is of course very important. I visited his riding and had an opportunity to listen to some very concerned and sympathetic people who discussed with me the difficulties they were having raising beef. It seemed to me, as I listened to them, that their problems were not with taxation but, rather, with high interest rates and low consumer prices. I asked whether relief from taxes would give them the relief they needed to survive, and their answer was no. They needed higher prices and some shelter from the economic storms that were hitting everyone.
If we were to follow the line of thought the Hon. Member has just given, we would have to start distinguishing between the activities of Canadians. We would have to say that farmers are a deserving group and should, therefore, be forgiven taxes. However, what about medical doctors? Are they not a useful, important group in our society? They must drive cars. Are they to be forgiven the fuel taxes on their vehicles if they drive to see a sick patient or to a hospital? Many people obviously do these important jobs. What is much more important here is to zero in on the economic problems from which the people are suffering and to try to solve those problems.
Let me point out to the Hon. Member to some of the activities of the Government. The $400 million extra injection into the Farm Credit Corporation is one good example of how we have attacked a basic problem by trying to shelter people from high interest rates, giving them relief under that Corporation. That, it seems to me, is a much better cure than a hodge podge on the tax system which discriminates in favour of one Canadian and against another, or chooses to artificially set taxes for one activity with none for another.
I thank the Hon. Member for reminding me of the importance of the farm community, but I must tell him that the cure he has proposed is not to be a genuine cure for the problems of the farmers.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR FREE VOTE ON ISSUE OF CRUISE MISSILE TESTING. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ALLOCATE DAY FOR DEBATE
REQUEST FOR FREE VOTE ON ISSUE OF CRUISE MISSILE TESTING. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ALLOCATE DAY FOR DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in response to a question of mine in the House of Commons, said he would welcome a debate on the Cruise missile test plans, yet he refused to allocate a Government day for that debate. He suggested that the New Democratic Party might use an opposition day for such a debate. I think he knew we had no opposition days left before the end of the year. The urgency of the debate is such that I do not believe we can wait until some time in the new year whenever that might be, and whenever the Conservatives might agree that we have such a debate on an opposition day.
The Government has been assuring us, through the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne), and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), that the new weapons agreement being drawn up in secret with the Pentagon is about to be signed-the framework agreement-and that the Cruise missile testing within that agreement has been agreed upon in principle, and the details will be worked out. This is imminent. In fact the Minister of National Defence said a couple of months ago in a letter to me that it would be within a few weeks. It could very well take place, therefore, during the Christmas adjournment. It was for this reason that I urged the Prime Minister to set aside a Government daysince we, as I say, do not have the NDP opposition day left before the end of the year. We have alrady used an opposition day on the Minority Report on Security and Disarmament. That debate did not deal with Cruise missile testing. The Prime Minister on that occasion said, as indeed he says will be true on every opposition day, that he will treat it as a vote of confidence and, therefore, will not allow a free vote.
The purpose of having a Government day with a resolution presented by the Government to the House delineating the framework agreement and the cruise missile testing agreement under it, is that the Government would not have to regard a vote on that as a vote of want of confidence. This would accomplish what the Prime Minister says he wants to accomplish, namely a debate, although I must says I have my doubts. He says he views the Cruise missile testing matter as extremely serious. This would give us the opportunity to have a debate.
I reminded the Prime Minister that the last time such a measure of magnitude in the field of defence was being undertaken, and agreement sought with the United States, was the NORAD agreement in 1958. This weapons testing agreement, nuclear weapons testing in particular, is the most significant matter, in my view and I think the view of all Members of the House, to come before us involving Canadian-American relations in matters of defence. At that time the Government of the day, under Mr. Diefenbaker, first of all said no to the Liberal opposition request for a Government resolution to bring the matter before the House. On May 19, 1958, Mr. Pearson, then the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition said:
Is it the intention of the government in respect of this very important intergovernmental agreement to follow the normal procedure of giving the house an opportunity, by the submission of a resolution, to express its views?
The then Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) in answer to that question replied:
-I would say no.
The next day, however, May 20, 1958, the Prime Minister of the day, Mr. Diefenbaker, did agree that on a matter of this importance there should be a Government resolution, that the matter should be debated and should come to a vote. That indeed, is what happened. That is the precedent I asked the Prime Minister to follow, and he has refused.
December 20, 1982
